patient.chief_complaint: Unable to be awakened after drinking, initial improvement then acute neurological deterioration
patient.history_present_illness: Ms. Katarina Novak is a 50-year-old right-handed woman brought to the emergency department at approximately 07:00 by her husband, who reports he was unable to awaken her that morning after she had consumed approximately one bottle of wine the prior evening. On initial evaluation, the patient was somnolent with moderate dysarthria, horizontal gaze-directed nystagmus, marked truncal ataxia, and bilateral upper and lower extremity incoordination. Given her known history of episodic heavy alcohol use, the clinical team initially attributed her symptoms to acute alcohol intoxication. Serum ethanol level returned at 2.3 per mille, consistent with significant intoxication. Forced diuresis was initiated, and the patient was placed on hourly neurological monitoring. By approximately 10:30, her clinical status appeared to improve substantially: she became more alert, her dysarthria resolved, and her ataxia improved significantly. However, at approximately 14:00, the nursing staff documented acute deterioration with rapidly worsening somnolence, new complaints of diplopia, difficulty swallowing, and recurrence of severe horizontal nystagmus and dysarthria. The patient's husband, who had remained at bedside, confirmed she had been conversant and sitting up comfortably just 30 minutes prior. There was no witnessed seizure activity, no head trauma, and no febrile illness. She had not vomited and there was no headache reported during her lucid interval. The pattern of initial improvement followed by sudden worsening raised concern for an evolving posterior circulation event rather than simple alcohol intoxication, prompting urgent re-evaluation. Of note, the family history is significant for early cerebrovascular disease in the mother, and the patient has a remote history of DVT.

results.title: Endovascular Therapy for Acute Basilar-Artery Occlusion (ATTENTION Trial)
results.authors: Tao C, Nogueira RG, et al.
results.key_finding: Endovascular thrombectomy within 12 hours of estimated occlusion time significantly improved functional outcomes compared to medical management alone in Chinese patients with acute basilar artery occlusion (mRS 0-3 at 90 days: 46% vs 23%).

results.title: Endovascular Therapy for Basilar-Artery Occlusion (BAOCHE Trial)
results.key_finding: Thrombectomy within 6-24 hours of estimated onset improved functional outcome in basilar artery occlusion patients selected by advanced imaging (mRS 0-3: 44% vs 25%).

results.title: Basilar Artery Occlusion: Clinical and Radiographic Predictors of Outcome
results.authors: Mattle HP, Arnold M, et al.
results.key_finding: Mortality in untreated basilar artery occlusion approaches 85-95%. Early recanalization is the strongest predictor of favorable outcome.

output.summary: Basilar artery occlusion is a neurovascular emergency with extremely high mortality without treatment. The ATTENTION (2023) and BAOCHE (2023) trials demonstrated clear benefit of endovascular thrombectomy within 12-24 hours of symptom onset, with improved rates of functional independence compared to medical therapy alone. Patient selection using advanced imaging (CTA, CT perfusion, or MRI) is critical. IV thrombolysis may be used as a bridge to thrombectomy. Fluctuating or stuttering symptoms are recognized presentations of basilar territory ischemia.

critical_actions: Establish time of last known well (LKW) and apply NIHSS to determine acute treatment eligibility
Obtain non-contrast CT head FIRST to exclude intracranial hemorrhage before any thrombolytic decision
Achieve door-to-needle time <60 minutes if IV thrombolysis is indicated
Maintain blood pressure <185/110 mmHg prior to IV tPA and <180/105 mmHg for 24 hours after
Verify glucose to exclude hypoglycemia as a stroke mimic
Initiate continuous telemetry and obtain prolonged cardiac monitoring to detect paroxysmal atrial fibrillation
Begin secondary prevention (antiplatelet or anticoagulation) and high-intensity statin per mechanism
Recognize basilar artery occlusion as a time-critical, thrombectomy-eligible diagnosis even in late-window presentations (ATTENTION, BAOCHE)
Activate stroke team and prepare for emergent mechanical thrombectomy
Empiric thiamine and glucose management for any alcohol-use-disorder patient with encephalopathy — do not delay imaging
Reassess any patient with focal deficits attributed to alcohol or sedatives — exam-imaging mismatch demands neuroimaging
contraindicated_actions: Do not administer IV tPA before non-contrast CT excludes intracranial hemorrhage
Do not give IV tPA if INR >1.7, platelet count <100,000, recent major surgery, or other guideline-listed contraindications
Do not aggressively lower blood pressure below 140/90 mmHg in the acute phase outside the tPA window — risks worsening penumbral perfusion
Do not delay non-contrast CT for additional imaging or labs in a stroke alert presentation
Do not start full-dose anticoagulation in the acute phase of a large infarct without considering hemorrhagic transformation risk
Do not anchor on alcohol intoxication when focal neurologic signs (gaze palsy, dysarthria, ataxia) persist or worsen — pursue immediate stroke imaging
Do not delay non-contrast CT and CTA on the basis of 'sobering up' the patient
key_reasoning_points: Acute ischemic stroke is a clinical syndrome plus neuroimaging diagnosis; CT first excludes hemorrhage and unmasks the tPA decision
Time of last known well governs IV thrombolysis eligibility (≤4.5h standard; selected up to 9h with imaging mismatch per WAKE-UP/EXTEND)
proximal vascular occlusion on CTA opens the mechanical thrombectomy pathway up to 24h per DAWN/DEFUSE-3 selection criteria
TOAST classification by mechanism (large-artery, cardioembolic, small-vessel, other, undetermined) drives secondary prevention strategy
Normal sinus rhythm on initial ECG does NOT exclude paroxysmal AF — extended cardiac monitoring is required, especially in cryptogenic stroke
Basilar artery occlusion is highly lethal without recanalization; thrombectomy benefit extends well beyond 24h in selected cases (ATTENTION, BAOCHE)
Posterior circulation strokes are commonly misdiagnosed because deficits (vertigo, dysarthria, gaze abnormalities) overlap with intoxication and benign vestibular conditions
HINTS-plus and a careful gaze/saccade examination help differentiate central from peripheral causes
Off-pathway modality for order_advanced_imaging (modality=amyloid_PET): Amyloid PET has no role in acute ischemic stroke evaluation and incurs substantial cost without altering management
Off-pathway modality for order_advanced_imaging (modality=DaTscan): Dopamine transporter SPECT is indicated for parkinsonian syndromes, not vascular stroke workup
Off-pathway modality for order_advanced_imaging (modality=FDG_PET): FDG-PET (neurodegenerative/oncologic indications) has no role in routine ischemic stroke workup

metadata.difficulty_description: Diagnostic puzzle — initial presentation mimics alcohol intoxication with elevated BAC, initial MRI is equivocal/falsely negative for posterior circulation stroke, and the critical diagnostic clue (fluctuating course and basilar artery occlusion) only emerges on follow-up evaluation and CTA. Multiple red herrings from alcohol-related lab abnormalities.
clinical_pearls: Posterior circulation strokes are missed more frequently than anterior circulation strokes because their symptoms (vertigo, ataxia, diplopia, dysarthria) overlap with common benign conditions and intoxication
DWI sensitivity for posterior circulation stroke in the first 24 hours is only 72-80%, compared to >95% for anterior circulation stroke
The 'stuttering' or fluctuating course in basilar artery occlusion results from intermittent collateral compensation and should trigger immediate vascular imaging
Approximately 25% of the general population has a PFO; its significance increases dramatically when combined with venous thrombosis history and thrombophilia
